title: Trump: Rudy Giuliani asks DHS to seize voting machines
description_short: Trump: Rudy Giuliani asks DHS to seize voting machines
description_medium: In December 2020, Rudy Giuliani asked Homeland Security official Ken Cuccinelli whether DHS could seize voting machines. Cuccinelli told him the department lacked that authority. The request came during efforts to challenge Donald Trump's defeat, but the exchange records a proposal and rejection, not a federal seizure.
description_long: In December 2020, Rudy Giuliani asked Ken Cuccinelli, then a senior Homeland Security official, whether the Department of Homeland Security could seize voting machines. Cuccinelli responded that DHS did not have that authority. The New York Times reported that Giuliani was weighing proposals to take control of voting equipment as part of efforts to reverse Donald Trump's election loss. The distinction between considering a seizure and carrying one out is important: this exchange did not result in DHS taking possession of machines. Election administration and equipment remained under state and local authority. CISA's role in protecting election infrastructure did not give it general power to confiscate voting systems at a campaign lawyer's request. The reported conversation illustrates how far Trump allies explored executive options after the 2020 vote, even when the officials they contacted said the government lacked the legal authority. It does not establish that the machines contained evidence capable of changing the result or that this particular request led to another action.

title: Trump: Jay Clayton tapped by Trump to lead SDNY
description_short: Trump: Jay Clayton tapped by Trump to lead SDNY
description_medium: On December 5, 2024, Donald Trump selected former Securities and Exchange Commission chair Jay Clayton to lead the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York. Reuters described Clayton as an unconventional choice because he had no criminal-law experience. His prior work with corporate clients raised questions about potential conflicts in an office that prosecutes financial crime.

Reuters reported that Clayton had no criminal-law experience, an unusual background for an office known for major financial-crime and public-corruption cases. His SEC work also involved a roster of corporate clients, creating potential overlap with companies that the SDNY could investigate. The New York Times had previously described the challenge of regulating businesses connected to Clayton's clients. The nomination therefore raised questions about experience and conflicts as well as the independence of a high-profile prosecutorial office. At the time of the announcement, this was a selection awaiting the appointment process, not proof that Clayton had taken office or altered any prosecution. title: Trump Administration cuts vaccine funds for poor countries
description_short: Trump Administration cuts vaccine funds for poor countries
description_medium: In March 2025, USAID sent Congress a list of foreign-assistance projects the Trump administration planned to stop funding. The proposed terminations included support for Gavi, which helps purchase vaccines for children in developing countries, and some malaria programs. State Department spokeswoman Tammy Bruce said awards were reviewed against administration priorities.
description_long: In March 2025, the U.S. Agency for International Development sent Congress a 281-page spreadsheet listing projects the administration planned to end. The list included funding for Gavi, an organization that helps countries obtain vaccines for children, as well as a reduction in support for malaria programs. The account listed 5,341 awards slated to end and 898 set to continue; these were planned terminations, not proof that every service had already stopped. State Department spokeswoman Tammy Bruce said awards were reviewed individually and ended when Secretary of State Marco Rubio found them inconsistent with agency or administration priorities. Sierra Leone's health minister, Austin Demby, warned that the decision could affect children's lives and global health security because his country relied on Gavi for vaccines. The funding changes also raised a legal question: Congress allocates money for individual health programs, and the administration's authority to cancel some awards was being challenged in court. The immediate event was a proposed retreat from foreign health assistance, with downstream effects dependent on implementation and litigation.

title: Donald Trump threatens to arrest Democrat Zohran Mamdani
description_short: Donald Trump threatens to arrest Democrat Zohran Mamdani
description_medium: On July 1, 2025, Donald Trump told reporters he would have New York City mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani arrested if Mamdani won the race and refused to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement. Trump also suggested Mamdani could be deported. Mamdani had just won the Democratic primary by 12 points.
description_long: On July 1, 2025, Donald Trump told reporters that he would have Zohran Mamdani arrested if Mamdani won New York City's mayoral election and refused to work with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Trump also suggested that Mamdani might become a target for deportation. The threat was conditional: Mamdani was then the Democratic nominee after winning the primary by 12 points, not yet the mayor. The Trump File account linked the remarks to video posted on social media and noted that Mamdani had received more votes than any New York City mayoral primary candidate in 36 years. title: Trump plans to deploy National Guard in Memphis
description_short: Trump plans to deploy National Guard in Memphis
description_medium: On September 12, 2025, Trump said on Fox News that he planned to send the National Guard to Memphis, replacing an earlier proposal to deploy troops in Chicago. Memphis Mayor Paul Young said he had not requested the deployment and opposed it; Trump had not notified him before announcing the plan.
description_long: Donald Trump announced on Fox News on September 12, 2025 that he intended to deploy the National Guard to Memphis, Tennessee, saying the city was “deeply troubled.” He framed the move as a change from an earlier plan to send troops to Chicago. Trump said Mayor Paul Young and Governor Bill Lee were happy with the decision. Young later said he had not requested the Guard and did not believe it was the way to reduce crime; he added that he had not been told of the decision before it was announced publicly. Young had spoken with Trump earlier in the week. The disagreement over local consent and public safety was central to the announcement. title: Trump Removes 9,500 US Troops from Germany Without NATO Consultation
description_short: Trump Removes 9,500 US Troops from Germany Without NATO Consultation
description_medium: In June 2020, the Trump administration announced it would withdraw approximately 9,500 US troops from Germany, reducing the force from about 34,500 to 25,000, without consulting NATO allies or Congress. Trump publicly said he was punishing Germany for being 'delinquent' on NATO spending commitments. Military commanders warned the withdrawal would weaken deterrence against Russia along NATO's eastern flank and damage decades of alliance infrastructure. German officials and US lawmakers of both parties condemned the decision.
description_long: In June 2020, the Trump administration announced a plan to withdraw about 9,500 U.S. troops from Germany, reducing the force from roughly 34,500 to 25,000. Trump said the move was punishment for Germany's failure to meet NATO's defense-spending target. Some of the troops were expected to be relocated to Poland. The announcement drew criticism from German officials and U.S. lawmakers in both parties, while military leaders warned that a rapid reduction could weaken deterrence on NATO's eastern flank and disrupt established alliance infrastructure. The proposal also raised concerns about coordination: Germany and other NATO allies said they had not been consulted in advance. The stated rationale focused on defense spending, but the NATO target is a shared commitment rather than a bill Germany owes directly to Washington. The plan represented a major change in U.S. force posture and in how the administration handled alliance policy. It should be understood as an announced reduction and repositioning; the announcement alone does not show that all 9,500 troops had already left or establish that it caused any later military conflict.

title: Donald Trump begins cultivating FBI agents in New York
description_short: Donald Trump begins cultivating FBI agents in New York
description_medium: A Trump File timeline says Donald Trump befriended New York FBI agent James Kallstrom after helping fund a 1973 Vietnam-veterans parade. It also reports later donations to Kallstrom's Marine Corps-Law Enforcement Foundation. The timeline's suggestion that these ties shaped FBI investigations requires corroboration.
description_long: A Trump File timeline places the start of Donald Trump's relationship with New York FBI agent James Kallstrom around 1973, when Kallstrom was organizing a parade for Vietnam veterans. It says Trump paid for much of the event and quotes Kallstrom recalling that Trump remained supportive of the bureau and helped with expenses after agents were injured. The account also reports that Trump later donated $1.3 million to the Marine Corps-Law Enforcement Foundation, which Kallstrom established in 1995. Those details describe a personal relationship and charitable support. They do not, by themselves, show that Trump became an FBI informant, received protection from investigators, or influenced any investigation. The timeline advances a broader theory about how such friendships could matter, but the timeline does not document a specific favor or official decision resulting from the relationship. The record is therefore useful as a reported account of Trump's early contact with an FBI official, while claims of corrupt influence require independent corroboration and a specific investigative outcome.

title: SNAP Loses 4 Million Participants Steepest Drop in 30 Years Under Big Beautiful Bill
description_short: SNAP Loses 4 Million Participants Steepest Drop in 30 Years Under Big Beautiful Bill
description_medium: More than 4 million Americans lost SNAP food assistance between July 2025 and March 2026, the steepest six-month decline since 1997, following HR 1 187 billion in SNAP cuts. The law expanded work requirements to adults ages 55-64, raised paperwork burdens, and for the first time required states to fund a share of SNAP benefits. Harvard public health professor Sara Naomi Bleich confirmed the drop reflects policy changes, not economic improvement, as unemployment remained flat.
description_long: Between July 2025 and March 2026, SNAP participation fell by more than four million people, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities and Reuters. The period followed enactment of H.R. 1, which reduced projected program spending by about $187 billion and changed eligibility and state cost-sharing rules. The law expanded work requirements to adults ages 55 through 64, increased paperwork obligations and required states to cover part of benefit costs. These provisions can affect whether eligible households continue receiving assistance, but the enrollment change does not show that every person left the program for the same reason. Harvard public-health professor Sara Naomi Bleich attributed the decline to policy changes rather than an improving economy and noted that unemployment remained flat. title: Trump Sweeps Super Tuesday Amid Mounting Controversies

His wins across states from Georgia to Massachusetts demonstrated his base was energized, not repelled, by controversy. Rival campaigns scrambled to mount a coordinated 'Stop Trump' effort. Republican establishment figures began contemplating a contested convention to deny Trump the nomination.
description_long: Donald Trump won seven of the eleven Republican contests held on Super Tuesday, March 1, 2016, extending his lead in the party's nomination race.
